source.title: AutoInterpretation Finds Sparse Coding Beats Alternatives

record.tranche_reason: The study compares automatic-interpretation scores across activation selections and scoring procedures, bearing on whether conclusions depend on how activations and explanations are measured.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates automatic-interpretation scores for learned features and several baselines; it does not directly count polysemantic neurons or test whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. Several score values appear only in figures, so they are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: It uses OpenAI auto-interpretation on Pythia-70M neuron-basis directions and shows their apparent interpretability changes with scoring. Residual-stream basis directions score high on top-and-random but explain no within-fragment variation. MLP neurons barely change when thresholded with bias+ReLU. This bears on V7 (measurement dependence). Most rows compare the authors' sparse-coding features with baselines, which is not a version's effect.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that sparse coding beats all tested baselines in MLP layer 1 and residual stream layer 2 (in the residual stream, under split scoring). They also conclude that top-and-random scoring is misleading for the residual stream, and that this supports linear features weakly anchored to the neuron basis. They call the results preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Uses OpenAI's automatic-interpretation procedure to compare sparse-coding directions and other feature dictionaries, rather than directly examining whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.method_sensitivity: For residual-stream features, the comparison changes between top-and-random scoring and separate top-only or random-only scoring. In the MLP, adding or removing bias and ReLU also changes the reported comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse-coding directions are more interpretable than the neuron basis, random directions, PCA and ICA in the MLP layer. In the residual stream this holds under split top-only and random-only scoring.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear features found by dictionary learning are more interpretable than individual neurons, consistent with features weakly anchored to the neuron basis.

record.problems: The authors describe the results as preliminary. Exact score values are not stated in the text and are presented in figures; the study tests automatic interpretability scores, not polysemantic-neuron frequency directly. The number of features varies between 40 and 150 per dictionary.
record.rows_left_out: PCA and ICA comparisons and other figure-only baseline scores were left out because they do not report a result about the tested measurement-dependence version beyond the rows retained. The study says PCA and ICA do not outperform the neuron basis, and that the first approximately 30 of 2048 PCA components tend to be highly interpretable.

untested.parts: No count or share of polysemantic MLP neurons.
No causal test of capacity pressure; only indirect evidence that learned directions beat neurons.
Initialization, regularization and noise are not studied.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
Only one explanation-scoring protocol, with its top/random splits. Neurons are never explicitly classified as polysemantic. A single model and two layers.

missing.what: Neuron-basis auto-interp scores in the residual stream: higher than MLP and random under top-and-random, but low to zero within fragments.
missing.locator: Residual Stream Results; Figures 4-6 and illustration

missing.what: MLP neuron basis with bias+ReLU: random-only scores perhaps rise slightly (top-and-random shows no noticeable change).
MLP neuron-basis top-only and random-only scores compared with top-and-random.

record.verdict_notes: This is a preliminary Alignment Forum post. All scores except one example are figure-only. Residual-stream basis directions are not MLP neurons, so the V7 support is indirect. Only one MLP dictionary was tested, with 40-150 features per dictionary.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns a language model, not image-classifier neurons.
It does not measure the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
It does not test whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
It does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemantic neurons.
It does not compare architectures or activation functions, or measure performance costs of lowering polysemanticity.
It does not investigate whether canonical mixed neuron responses share a feature.
It varies activation selection and automatic-interpretation scoring, but does not directly classify neurons as polysemantic or test other explanation-scoring methods.

source_check.notes: Preliminary LessWrong post: GPT-4 explainer, GPT-3.5 simulator, 40 to 150 'first' features per dictionary. All values are figure-only. It measures auto-interp scores, not polysemanticity directly. The text says 'no noticeable improvement' (not 'change') for top-and-random. Rows r5-r7 compare the study's own sparse coding with baselines and are linked to none. The residual-stream neuron-basis V7 finding has no row.

statements.problem: none. The text's exact wording is 'no noticeable improvement' for top-and-random. The slight random-only rise is attributed correctly.

statements.correction: Auto-interp is run on 40 to 150 features per dictionary (the 'first' ones), not the whole neuron basis. Reports mean score with 95% CIs, figure only. GPT-4 explainer, GPT-3.5 simulator. Top-and-random: no noticeable improvement from bias+ReLU.
statements.problem: differences_stated says the study 'scores the whole neuron basis'. It scores only 40 to 150 'first' features per dictionary, out of 2048 MLP neurons.

statements.correction: One explainer (GPT-4) and one simulator (GPT-3.5). Three score splits compared (top-and-random, top-only, random-only). No individual neurons are classified as polysemantic.
statements.problem: 'One scoring protocol' is loose. The study compares top-and-random, top-only and random-only scoring, which is the 'how explanations are scored' part of V7. The single-judge point holds: there is one explainer (GPT-4) and one simulator (GPT-3.5).

statements.correction: Bias+ReLU on the neuron basis and random directions, Pythia-70M MLP layer 1: no noticeable improvement in top-and-random score. Random-only scores perhaps rise slightly. Figure only; preliminary.
statements.problem: Leaves out the scoring condition. 'No noticeable improvement' holds only for top-and-random, and the text says random-only scores perhaps rise slightly with bias+ReLU.
